study.title: Revelation 18 The fall of Babylon and the judgment of God
study.overview: The chapter presents the fall of Babylon as a fact decreed by God and announced with poetic and solemn language. The city, or system represented by Babylon, is described as corrupt, seductive, violently and economically powerful, but destined for sudden ruin. The text contrasts the grief of those who profited from it with the joy of heaven, because God finally judges the cause of his saints.

outline.title: Announcement of Babylon's fall
outline.explanation: An angel descends from heaven and proclaims that Babylon fell. The description shows the city as a place of spiritual impurity, influence over nations and enrichment based on sensuality and corruption.

outline.title: Call to go out and divine sentence
outline.explanation: A voice from heaven calls God's people to depart from the city so that they may not share their sins or their plagues. The text explains that Babylon's guilt has come to the fullest and that his judgment will come suddenly in one day.

outline.title: I'm sorry of those who profited from her
outline.explanation: Kings, merchants, captains and sailors cry in the distance. They lament not the wickedness of Babylon, but the loss of trade, wealth and prestige they received from it. The list of goods shows luxury, exploitation and even human trafficking.

outline.title: Joy of the sky and final ruin
outline.explanation: Heaven is called to rejoice because God has done justice for the sake of the saints. A stone thrown into the sea symbolizes the violent and irreversible destruction of Babylon, whose cultural, commercial and festive life will cease. The chapter ends up accusing it with innocent blood and deceiving the nations.

study.context: The notes provided treat Babylon as a symbolic figure, and some relate it to Rome, but they also recognize other historical applications in debate. The chapter uses images of lament and judgment already present in the Old Testament prophets, especially in denunciations against proud and oppressive cities. The notes by Tyndale and Adam Clarke highlight the poetic character of rebuke and the theme of complete and irreversible destruction.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that God sees corruption hidden behind the economic brightness and political prestige. The wealth obtained by unjust means, moral seduction and persecution of God's servants do not go unnoticed. The divine judgment is right, proportional and sudden. At the same time, the call to leave the city shows that God's people should not share the moral complicity of foreign sin. The contrast between the mourning of the allies of Babylon and the joy of heaven reveals that the righteousness of God is a reason for comfort for the saints. The mention of the blood of the prophets and saints shows that opposition to God has accumulated moral weight and will be punished.

scholarViews.insight: The angel receives his brightness from heaven, and the word used for this splendor is usually linked to the divine presence; this reinforces that the proclamation of the fall comes with heavenly authority.
The command to leave Babylon shows that God's people should not share in their sins or receive their plagues; there is moral separation before judgment.
The list of commodities includes human bodies and souls, indicating that the trade of Babylon involves extreme exploitation and even human trafficking.

questions: What areas of culture, consumption or power can try us to participate in the same corruption that Babylon represents?
How does the call to get out of it confronts practical commitments, not just internal beliefs?
When we see injustice and oppression seem victorious, how does God's final judgment change our perspective?
study.practice: Reading of this chapter calls for discernment and moral separation. The Christian should examine where he is receiving pleasure, security or profit from unjust structures, and renounce any complicity with sin. It is also an invitation to maintain hope when evil seems strong: Babylon's fall shows that the final word does not belong to the corrupted system, but to God. In practice, this implies living with simplicity, fidelity to the gospel and compassion for those who suffer under systems of exploitation.
study.uncertainty: The exact identification of Babylon remains interpretive in the notes provided: they relate it mainly to Rome, but they also mention other proposed applications. The chapter uses symbolic and poetic language; therefore, some details should be read as images of judgment, not as literal descriptions of a specific city in all respects.
